details.notes_vi: Tham khảo Part 5, 6, 7 và dạng một/nhiều văn bản. Trang ghi rõ đề mẫu và chỉ dẫn thuộc bản quyền ETS, cần sự cho phép khi sao chép.

sources.title: Preparation Materials for the TOEIC Tests

details.notes_vi: Có handbook và sample tests. Giữ link ngoài; không tái đăng câu hỏi hoặc PDF ETS trong database.
Tham khảo hoạt động đọc và chủ đề phù hợp trẻ nhỏ. Level 1/2/3 của trang không được tự động xem là CEFR của trẻ.

sample_resources.title: School note
sample_resources.observed_format: School notice with preparation, reading exercises and answer download. Metadata only; text not imported.

details.notes_vi: Nguồn đọc phân cấp A1–C1 và bài tập dành cho thiếu niên. Dùng tham khảo cách chia cấp và kỹ năng.

sample_resources.title: Foreign exchange emails
sample_resources.observed_format: B1 email reading, true/false comprehension and matching informal expressions. Metadata only; text not imported.

details.notes_vi: Các nhóm hoạt động Pre A1, A1, A2 cho trẻ; chọn độ khó theo năng lực thay vì đồng nhất tuổi với CEFR.
Tham khảo tài liệu chuẩn bị A2 Key và các liên kết cho Schools. Bài của bộ seed là luyện đọc phổ thông, không phải đề Cambridge chính thức.
Tham khảo kỹ năng mức B1. Không coi đây là nguồn xác nhận cấu trúc đề tốt nghiệp THPT Việt Nam.
Các nhóm đọc A1–C1, đa dạng dạng văn bản như thông báo, email, bài báo và báo cáo.

sample_resources.title: A poster at work
sample_resources.observed_format: A1 event invitation with two follow-up tasks. Metadata only; text not imported.

details.notes_vi: Có nhóm A1–A2 và B1–B2, chia theo chủ đề. Không sao chép định nghĩa, ảnh, audio hoặc câu hỏi.
Có bộ lọc kỹ năng, khoảng trình độ và thời lượng; tham khảo thiết kế hoạt động ngắn.
Nguồn tham khảo để biên tập viên đối chiếu từ loại/cấp độ khi mở rộng. Không sao chép toàn bộ danh sách hay định nghĩa; CEFR trong seed là ước lượng biên soạn, chưa được đối chiếu từng từ với Oxford.

Kết quả chỉ mục chính thức nêu CC BY 4.0. Mở trang trực tiếp bị chặn khi khảo sát; chưa lấy truyện cụ thể. Khi nhập truyện, kiểm tra trang quyền của đúng truyện và ghi tác giả, họa sĩ, nguồn, giấy phép, thay đổi. Không coi nhãn toàn kho thay cho kiểm tra từng mục.
Kết quả tìm kiếm phân biệt sách CC BY 4.0 với các tài sản khác như video/readalong; chưa nhập file hay tranh từ nền tảng.
ETS yêu cầu quyền bằng văn bản khi tái bản tài liệu thuộc bản quyền. Lưu nguồn để quản lý quyền sử dụng nội dung ngoài.
Chính sách cấp phép TOEIC và điều kiện sử dụng. Bộ seed không nhập đề ETS và không suy diễn quyền tái bản từ việc có thể tải miễn phí.
CC BY 4.0 cho phép chia sẻ/chỉnh sửa cả mục đích thương mại với điều kiện tương ứng như ghi công, dẫn giấy phép, chỉ rõ chỉnh sửa. Chỉ áp dụng cho tài sản thực sự được cấp phép.
Nguồn mở có hạn chế phi thương mại và ngoại lệ tài sản bên thứ ba. Không đưa vào luồng nhập tự động cho website có thu phí/quảng cáo nếu chưa làm rõ điều kiện.

passages.text: When the imagined town of Willow opened a library of things, its shelves held drills, sewing machines and camping equipment rather than books. The idea came from residents who owned useful objects but used them only occasionally. They wanted their neighbours to borrow these objects instead of buying another copy. The library began in a spare room beside the community hall. Although the room was small, its central location meant that residents could collect an item on their way home from work.

passages.label: B
passages.text: At first, volunteers accepted every donation. This approach soon caused problems: some objects had missing parts, while others needed expensive repairs. The team therefore introduced an inspection before accepting equipment. A volunteer now checks each item and records its condition. Members pay an annual fee, but the fee does not change with the number of loans. A refundable deposit is required only for the most expensive items. Instructions are attached to every object, including those that appear simple to use.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The organisers expected power tools to be the most popular category. During the first summer, however, demand for folding tables was greater. Families borrowed them for celebrations, and local clubs used them for meetings. This unexpected pattern changed the purchasing plan. Instead of adding more drills, the team bought tables that could be stored flat. Members can reserve items online, but telephone bookings remain available because some residents do not use the internet. No member receives priority simply for making an online reservation.

passages.label: D
passages.text: The project also changed the volunteers' understanding of success. They initially counted loans, but a high total did not show whether people were learning to maintain equipment. They added short repair workshops and began asking members what they had learned. These answers were useful, although not every member completed the questionnaire. The library does not claim that all shared objects last longer than privately owned ones. Its more modest aim is to make useful equipment accessible and help residents feel confident about using it.

passages.label: A
passages.text: At the fictional Brook School, a flat roof above the dining room became a garden. The teachers did not begin by ordering plants. They first asked an engineer to check the roof, because soil and water would add weight to the building. After this assessment, they selected lightweight containers and kept a clear path to the exit. The first planting area occupied only one corner. Starting small allowed the school to discover practical difficulties before expanding the project to a larger space.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Pupils initially wanted colourful flowers everywhere, but the garden committee chose a mixture of flowers and vegetables. Each class adopted one container and kept a diary of changes. Some pupils measured stems, while others drew leaves or recorded the weather. The diary was not a competition to produce the tallest plant. Teachers wanted pupils to notice differences and explain them carefully. A small plant could therefore provide an interesting lesson, particularly if its container received less sunlight than a neighbouring one.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Watering proved harder to organise than planting. During term time, pupils followed a weekly rota. The holiday period was different: the building remained open to staff, but pupils were away. The committee invited local volunteers to help, and each volunteer received a key for an agreed afternoon. A simple chart beside the entrance showed when each container had last been watered. This prevented two visitors from watering the same plants unnecessarily. The school chose not to install an automatic watering system in the first year.

passages.label: D
passages.text: At the end of the year, the vegetables supplied just one small school lunch. The garden was therefore not a serious source of food for the dining room. Nevertheless, the teachers judged the project worthwhile. Pupils had used measurements in a real setting and had learned that a shared space required regular attention. The committee planned to add more containers, but only after arranging enough help for the next holiday. For this school, a larger garden would be useful only if the existing routine remained manageable.

passages.label: A
passages.text: In the imagined district of Northbridge, a stream once flowed through an underground pipe beneath a shopping street. A redevelopment proposal brought an unusual question to public meetings: should part of the stream be visible again? Supporters described a narrow channel lined with plants, while opponents worried about losing delivery space. Neither group disputed the need to replace the old pipe. Their disagreement concerned what should happen above it and whose daily routines the new design should prioritise.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The first drawing showed a continuous open channel. However, shopkeepers explained that delivery vehicles needed to stop beside particular entrances. The design team revised the plan, retaining covered crossings at those locations. Pedestrians would still see much of the water, but the stream would not be uncovered everywhere. This compromise reduced the area available for planting. It also made the proposal easier to support, because traders could recognise their own requirements in the revised drawing rather than simply being told that the project would benefit everybody.

passages.label: C
passages.text: A second challenge involved maintenance. The attractive images used at public meetings showed clear water and tidy plants, but they did not explain who would remove fallen leaves. The district therefore prepared a maintenance agreement before construction began. Street cleaners would check the crossings, while a gardening team would look after the planted edges. The agreement also identified a contact person for residents reporting problems. Officials argued that the stream should be treated as working infrastructure, not merely as a decorative feature for opening day.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Once the channel opened, the district compared photographs taken from fixed points each month. These images revealed changes in the plants but could not establish whether the project had improved business. A nearby shop reported higher sales, yet its owner had also extended the opening hours. The two changes could not be separated by looking at sales figures alone. The district consequently described the commercial outcome as uncertain. Residents could enjoy the new space without every claimed benefit having been demonstrated, and future evaluations would need evidence suited to each separate question.

passages.label: A
passages.text: The imaginary Harbour Museum owns a collection of fragile pottery. Its visitors can see the original bowls through glass, but the cases reveal little about their weight or texture. To address this limitation, the museum commissioned replicas that visitors could handle. The aim was not to replace the originals or to make perfect copies for sale. Instead, the education team wanted visitors to explore qualities that photographs and labels could describe only indirectly, while keeping the historical objects protected from repeated contact.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Making a useful replica required choices. A visually exact copy made from a different material might feel much lighter than the original. Conversely, a copy with an accurate weight could have a surface that was too smooth. The museum therefore created two versions of one bowl: one reproduced its appearance, and another approximated its weight and roughness. Each was labelled to explain its purpose. This solution made the limitations visible rather than allowing visitors to assume that every copy reproduced all the qualities of the original.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Guides initially handed out replicas near the end of each tour. They later moved the activity to the beginning, asking visitors to describe what they noticed before hearing an explanation. The change encouraged questions about how the bowls might have been carried and stored. Visitors were not invited to guess the exact age of a bowl from its weight. The guides explained that handling a replica could generate questions, but a reliable historical conclusion required other evidence as well. Touch became an entry point for investigation rather than a shortcut to certainty.

passages.label: D
passages.text: The museum evaluated the activity by recording the range of questions visitors asked. It also offered an alternative description for people who preferred not to handle objects. Staff resisted measuring success only by how many replicas were picked up, since an object might be handled briefly without attracting much attention. The most useful feedback concerned connections between physical experience and the display. Some visitors returned to the glass cases to look again. Their return did not prove that they had learned every historical detail, but it suggested that the handling activity had given them a reason to examine the originals more closely.

passages.label: A
passages.text: Imagine a regional seed collection established to support community gardens. At first glance, its labelled packets might resemble an ordinary store cupboard. Yet keeping seeds useful requires more than arranging them neatly. The collection must retain information about where each sample came from, how it was grown and when it was harvested. Without those records, a packet may still contain living seeds, but gardeners have less basis for deciding whether the plants are suitable for a particular place or purpose.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The fictional Greenfield collection initially accepted seeds from anyone who offered them. Its staff soon found that the same local name sometimes referred to different plants. They introduced a registration form asking donors to describe the plant as well as name it. Photographs were helpful, but they did not replace written observations. Where identification remained uncertain, the packet was stored separately until a specialist could inspect it. This procedure slowed the arrival of new samples but reduced confusion in the collection.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Storage created another challenge. Staff could not assume that every packet would remain usable indefinitely. At planned intervals, they took a small sample from selected packets and checked whether the seeds would germinate. A poor result triggered further testing rather than an immediate decision to throw everything away. Some seeds might need different conditions to begin growing. The collection therefore recorded the testing method alongside the result. A number without this explanation could suggest a clear answer while hiding an important difference between tests.

passages.label: D
passages.text: The gardeners who received seeds were also invited to contribute information. They reported when plants flowered and described any difficulties, making the collection a growing record of local experience. However, staff did not treat every report as equally informative. A crop that failed after a container dried out said little about how the same plant would perform in well-watered soil. The purpose was not to dismiss disappointing results, but to preserve enough context to interpret them. The collection's most valuable resource was therefore not simply a large number of packets; it was the connection between the seeds and the knowledge that accompanied them.

passages.label: A
passages.text: A fictional neighbourhood group in Ashford wanted to understand differences in air quality along the route to school. It could not purchase a professional monitoring station, so it borrowed several small sensors. The devices displayed a reading every minute and were easy to carry. Their convenience was attractive, but the group did not assume that a number on a screen was automatically an accurate measurement. Before collecting data outdoors, members placed the sensors together in the same room to compare their readings.

passages.label: B
passages.text: One device consistently showed higher values than the others. The group did not solve this problem by deleting every reading from that sensor. Instead, it recorded the difference and sought advice on calibration. Members also agreed on a common procedure: walk the same route at the same time of day and pause at specified locations. This reduced some variation between trips, although it could not remove all the effects of weather or changing traffic. A consistent method made comparisons more meaningful without making the measurements perfect.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The first map appeared to show a strong contrast between a busy junction and a quiet lane. Some members wanted to publish it immediately as proof that the lane was always safer. Others pointed out that the measurements covered only two mornings. They returned on further days, adding notes about roadworks and unusual queues. The additional observations did not simply confirm the first picture: the contrast was smaller on some visits. The final display therefore included the dates and range of readings instead of a single coloured label for each street.

passages.label: D
passages.text: At a community meeting, the group used its findings to ask the transport department for more detailed monitoring. It did not present the sensor map as a medical assessment or as a substitute for professional equipment. Its contribution lay partly in identifying questions that residents wanted answered. The exercise had also taught participants to discuss uncertainty openly. A limitation, they learned, was not necessarily a reason to abandon data collection. It was a reason to describe the method clearly and to keep conclusions within what the evidence could support.

passages.label: A
passages.text: Imagine an archive collecting memories of a former textile factory. The first volunteers are retired managers, whose names are easy to find in company records. Their interviews describe business decisions in detail. However, an archive built only from these interviews would offer a narrow account of factory life. Cleaners, temporary workers and nearby residents might remember different aspects of the same place. The problem is not that the managers' memories are necessarily false. It is that availability should not be mistaken for completeness.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The fictional archive team therefore changes its recruitment method. Rather than sending invitations only to known contacts, it places notices in local shops and holds an open afternoon at a community centre. Interviewers explain that ordinary routines matter as much as dramatic events. They ask about journeys to work, meal breaks and the sounds inside the building. These questions help people who initially believe that they have nothing important to contribute. Participation remains voluntary, and no contributor is required to agree with an earlier interview.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Memories sometimes conflict. Two workers may describe the same room differently because they used it in different years. The team keeps both accounts and records when each person worked there. Where a date cannot be established, the uncertainty is noted rather than removed from the transcript. Written records may clarify a point, but they are not assumed to contain every relevant detail. The aim is to make disagreement understandable, not to manufacture one smooth story by deleting everything that fails to fit.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Access raises a further question. A person may willingly describe a difficult experience to an interviewer but not want the recording immediately available online. The archive offers contributors a choice: public access, a restricted period, or use only within the research team. These options may make the collection less convenient for some users, yet convenience alone is an inadequate reason to ignore consent. An archive earns trust through the way it treats people as well as through the amount of material it holds. Preserving a voice should not mean taking away the speaker's control over its use.

passages.label: A
passages.text: In an imaginary hospital, the facilities team receives repeated comments about a noisy waiting room. The room contains no unusually loud machine. Instead, several ordinary sounds overlap: conversations, an announcement speaker and chairs moving across the floor. Replacing one device would therefore be unlikely to solve the whole problem. The team begins by observing where and when the sounds occur. It treats the complaints as a design question about the shared environment, without claiming that a quieter room would by itself improve any medical condition.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The first proposal is to lower the volume of announcements. Reception staff object because some visitors already struggle to hear their names. A solution that seems comfortable to one person could make the service harder to use for another. The team keeps the spoken announcements but adds a screen showing the same information. It also moves the speaker away from a corner where its sound is reflected across the room. Visitors can choose seats close to the screen if they prefer to follow the visual display.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Furniture creates a separate difficulty. Heavy chairs scrape when moved, but fixing every chair to the floor would prevent families from arranging seats together. The team instead tests protective pads under a small group of chairs. Cleaning staff check whether the pads remain secure after the floor is washed. This detail matters because a design that works during a demonstration may fail during ordinary maintenance. The trial continues for several weeks before the team decides whether to use the pads throughout the room.

passages.label: D
passages.text: To assess the changes, the hospital combines sound measurements with visitor comments. Neither source tells the whole story. A lower average sound level might conceal a few sudden announcements that people find disturbing. Conversely, favourable comments might reflect a shorter waiting time rather than a change in the room itself. Staff therefore note how busy the room is and how long people wait when collecting feedback. The purpose is not to produce one impressive number, but to understand which changes help different users and under what circumstances.

passages.label: A
passages.text: A fictional design class receives a simple challenge: create a cardboard carrier that protects three glass jars during a short journey. Students immediately begin discussing shapes and handles. Their tutor interrupts with a different request. Before building anything, each group must state what it expects its design to achieve and how that expectation could be tested. A carrier that looks elegant is not necessarily useful. The class needs a way to judge performance that does not depend entirely on the enthusiasm of the people who made it.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The first trial uses empty jars. Several carriers survive, giving their creators confidence. The tutor then asks whether this is a fair representation of the intended task. In actual use, the jars would contain food and weigh more. The groups repeat the trial with a standard load. Some handles tear, while other structures bend without breaking. The change does not make the first trial worthless; it reveals the limited question that the earlier test could answer. It had examined the carriers under a lighter load, not established their suitability for every journey.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Students respond to failure in different ways. One group adds layers of cardboard everywhere, producing a stronger but awkward carrier. Another traces the tear to a narrow join and reinforces only that area. Both designs improve on one measure, but their effects on material use and comfort differ. The tutor asks groups to record their modifications and the reasons for them. A list of changes without an explanation would show activity, but it would reveal little about the students' developing understanding.

passages.label: D
passages.text: For the final discussion, each group presents a successful carrier alongside an earlier version that failed. The assessment rewards clear reasoning about the comparison as well as the performance of the finished object. This approach does not mean that failure is automatically educational. A broken prototype becomes informative only when someone investigates why it broke and chooses the next test accordingly. Equally, success should invite questions: a carrier that survives one careful journey may still fail when hurried users lift it differently. Design learning continues when a result is treated as evidence with boundaries, rather than as a final verdict.

passages.label: A
passages.text: Consider an imagined project digitising a handwritten travel journal. A clean transcription would make the journal searchable, but producing one is not simply a matter of replacing handwriting with typed letters. The writer crossed out words, inserted remarks between lines and occasionally used a mark that could be read in more than one way. If the digital edition silently resolves every ambiguity, it may appear more authoritative than the surviving document warrants. Readability and fidelity are related aims, but they do not invariably point towards the same editorial decision.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The project team rejects the idea of one definitive display. Instead, it offers a reading view with expanded abbreviations and a documentary view that preserves line breaks and visible corrections. Users can move between these views and inspect an image of the relevant page. The distinction is not between a true text and a false one: both are interpretations governed by stated rules. The reading view prioritises continuity, whereas the documentary view makes features of the writing process easier to examine.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Disputed words require a further mechanism. Editors attach alternatives to the uncertain passage and explain the evidence for each. A later decision does not erase an earlier interpretation; the edition keeps a revision history. This record enables a researcher to understand why a quotation in an older article differs from the current display. It also prevents the latest version from concealing the intellectual work behind it. The cost is additional complexity, which the team manages by showing short notes first and allowing readers to open fuller explanations when needed.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Such transparency does not remove the need for editorial judgement. Someone still chooses which alternatives are plausible enough to display and how much evidence a note should include. Nor does showing an original page guarantee that every reader can interpret the handwriting. Nevertheless, an edition that exposes its decisions gives users a better basis for questioning them. Its authority rests less on the appearance of finality than on the traceability of its reasoning. For this project, a useful digital text is therefore neither an unmediated copy nor a permanently settled answer, but a structured invitation to examine how knowledge about a document has been made.

passages.label: A
passages.text: Imagine three farming communities drawing water from the same small reservoir. For many years, an informal arrangement gives each community a fixed day of access. The schedule is easy to remember and is regarded as fair because every group receives equal time. However, equal time need not yield an equal volume of water. When pressure falls later in the week, the last community fills its channels more slowly. A rule can remain unchanged while its consequences become increasingly uneven.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Representatives propose replacing fixed days with measured allocations. This appears to offer greater precision, but it introduces new disputes. Someone must decide how much water each community needs, where the meters should be placed and who will check them. The communities also cultivate different crops, so a uniform allocation may affect them differently. A technical device can measure a flow, but it cannot independently determine what distribution ought to count as fair. That judgement requires an agreement about priorities as well as reliable information.

passages.label: C
passages.text: In this fictional case, the communities retain the weekly schedule but rotate the order of access each month. They also establish a review meeting after unusually dry periods. The arrangement is deliberately provisional: it can be revised when participants explain a problem that the existing rule does not address. Records of withdrawals are shared, but individual complaints are not automatically accepted as proof of unfairness. Representatives compare them with the records and invite affected neighbours to explain what happened. This process takes time, yet it reduces reliance on accusations that cannot be examined.

passages.label: D
passages.text: The example illustrates why durable cooperation is not always produced by a rule that anticipates every possible condition. Such a rule might become too complicated to understand or enforce. Cooperation may instead depend on a credible way to question and amend a simpler rule. That does not mean that agreements should change whenever one participant dislikes an outcome. Predictability still matters. The challenge is to combine a stable starting point with a legitimate process for revision, so that flexibility serves a shared purpose rather than becoming a privilege available only to the most influential users.

passages.label: A
passages.text: A fictional museum receives a nineteenth-century map of a coastal district. Roads and warehouses are carefully drawn, yet a large area behind the harbour is almost blank. A visitor might conclude that nobody lived there. The curator cautions against that inference. A map is a selective representation made for a purpose, not a transparent inventory of everything that existed. Before treating an omission as evidence of absence, the researcher needs to ask what the mapmaker was trying to record and what lay outside that task.

passages.label: B
passages.text: An accompanying letter indicates that the map was commissioned to support a proposal for moving goods from ships to a railway station. This explains the prominence of roads and storage buildings. Houses were relevant only where they obstructed a proposed route. The map's silence about other homes was therefore a consequence of its function, rather than a deliberate statement that those homes did not exist. Recognising that function changes the questions a researcher can reasonably expect the document to answer.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The curator compares the map with household lists and a later drawing by a local resident. These sources suggest that small dwellings occupied part of the apparently empty area. They do not, however, permit an exact reconstruction of every building. The lists record occupants but rarely describe positions, while the drawing compresses distances to fit the page. Combining imperfect sources does not automatically remove their weaknesses. It can nevertheless reveal where one source supplies information that another was never designed to include.

passages.label: D
passages.text: For the exhibition, the museum overlays the old map with a shaded zone indicating possible residential occupation. It avoids drawing precise house outlines that the evidence cannot justify. A caption distinguishes between documented features, plausible interpretation and unresolved questions. This restraint may make the display less immediately satisfying than a complete reconstruction, but it protects an essential distinction: what can be imagined is not identical to what can be established. The map becomes valuable not because it tells the whole story, but because its inclusions and omissions can be examined alongside other traces of the past.

passages.text:
Harbour Café: Staff notice
From 6 May, Harbour Café will open at 7 a.m. instead of 8 a.m. on weekdays. Several nearby offices have asked for an earlier breakfast service. Weekend opening hours will remain unchanged. The change will be tested for four weeks, after which the manager will review sales and staff feedback before deciding whether to continue it.
During the trial, two employees will begin work at 6:30 a.m. to prepare drinks and display baked goods. Volunteers for these early shifts should contact Mina by Friday. Staff who take an early shift will finish one hour earlier than usual; their total working hours will not increase. If too few employees volunteer, Mina will discuss a rotating schedule with the team.
The full breakfast menu will be available from opening time. However, deliveries from the bakery will still arrive at 7:30 a.m., so the first customers will be offered items prepared in the café. Do not promise that bakery croissants will be available before the delivery arrives.
A short training session on the new opening checklist will be held after closing on Thursday. Attendance is required only for employees assigned to the early shifts. The checklist will also be posted beside the coffee machine for reference. Please send any suggestions about the trial to Mina in writing.

passages.label: D1
passages.text:
Northbank Workspace: Flexible memberships
Northbank Workspace offers shared desks and private meeting rooms for small businesses. The building is open to members from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. Monday to Saturday. Reception support is available from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.; members arriving outside those hours must use their access card.
The Flex membership costs 90 credits per month and includes six desk visits. Each visit allows up to four hours at a shared desk. Additional visits cost 18 credits each. The Resident membership costs 180 credits per month and includes unlimited desk visits during opening hours, plus two hours of meeting-room use. Neither plan includes a reserved personal desk.
Meeting rooms must be booked separately through the member portal. Unused included hours do not carry over into the next month. Members on either plan may bring one guest to a booked meeting room, but guests may not occupy shared desks.
New members can try one desk visit free of charge before selecting a plan. The trial must be booked in advance and is offered only while reception is staffed. After joining, members may change their plan for the following month by submitting a request at least five days before renewal. Memberships renew automatically unless cancelled through the portal. A free orientation is available every Wednesday for anyone who wants to see the facilities before applying.

passages.label: D1
passages.text:
Riverstone Training Rooms: Booking policy
Room Pine seats up to twenty people and includes a projector. Room Cedar seats up to thirty-five and includes a projector and two whiteboards. Rooms can be reserved for either a morning session, 9 a.m. to noon, or an afternoon session, 1 p.m. to 5 p.m.
A booking may be cancelled for a full refund at least forty-eight hours before its start time. Between twenty-four and forty-eight hours before the start, customers may move the booking once to an available date within the same month, but no refund is offered. Changes requested less than twenty-four hours before the start cannot be accepted.
Refreshments must be ordered separately at least two working days in advance. Customers may bring their own drinking water, but outside meals are not permitted. All room changes require written confirmation from our booking team.

passages.label: D2
passages.text:
To: Riverstone booking team
Sent: Monday 10 June, 10 a.m.
Subject: Tuesday 11 June afternoon reservation
We have reserved Room Cedar for Tuesday 11 June at 1 p.m. for a group of twenty-eight. Our trainer is unexpectedly unavailable, so we would like to move the session to the afternoon of Thursday 13 June. I checked your calendar, and Cedar is shown as available then. We still need the projector and both whiteboards. We have not ordered refreshments and will bring bottled water. Please let me know whether the change is possible before I notify the participants.
Regards,
Elena Duarte

passages.label: D1
passages.text:
Clearview Displays: Product and delivery guide
The Compact stand holds a screen up to twenty-four inches and folds into a carrying case. It weighs three kilograms and is available immediately. The Tall stand holds a screen up to thirty-two inches and has a shelf for printed material. It weighs seven kilograms. New stock of the Tall stand will arrive on 18 June; we cannot dispatch it earlier.
Orders placed by noon on 10 June can use one of two delivery services: standard delivery arriving on 15 June, included in the listed price, or express delivery arriving on 12 June for an additional fee. We do not provide weekend deliveries. Collection from our depot is also possible during weekday office hours, but only after a collection confirmation has been sent.
All stands carry a one-year warranty against manufacturing faults. Screen equipment is not included.

passages.label: D2
passages.text:
To: Clearview sales team
Subject: Display stand for recruitment fair
We need a stand for our twenty-two-inch screen at a recruitment fair on 14 June. It must arrive at our office by 13 June because we will pack the van that afternoon. We do not need a shelf, and a lighter stand would be preferable. We can place the order and pay before noon on 10 June, but nobody can visit your depot. Please recommend a model and delivery option that meet these requirements.
Thank you,
Omar Lewis

passages.label: D1
passages.text:
Orchard Conference Centre: Wednesday programme
Registration opens in the main lobby at 9 a.m. The data workshop begins at 9:30 a.m. in Oak Room and lasts one hour. Participants should bring a laptop with the sample files downloaded in advance. At 11 a.m., a product demonstration will take place in Elm Room. No equipment is required for this demonstration, and printed catalogues will be provided at the entrance.
Lunch will be served on the terrace at noon. The afternoon customer-feedback discussion starts at 1 p.m. in Oak Room. Participants may attend any session for which they have registered. Please check the noticeboard in the lobby for last-minute changes to locations.

passages.label: D2
passages.text:
To: Registered participants
Sent: Tuesday evening
Subject: Room changes for Wednesday
A water leak has made Oak Room unavailable for the whole of Wednesday. The data workshop will move to Birch Room. Since Birch is smaller, only the first eighteen people on the workshop registration list can attend there. A live video stream will be shown in Willow Room for the remaining registered participants. Both rooms will allow participants to submit questions to the instructor.
The customer-feedback discussion will move to Elm Room at its original time. All other programme items remain unchanged. The revised room list will be displayed at the main entrance. We apologise for the disruption.

passages.label: D3
passages.text:
Wednesday staff chat
Leon, 8:45 a.m.: I am nineteenth on the data workshop registration list. Does the overflow video have captions? I find them helpful when taking notes.
Jia, 8:47 a.m.: Yes. The event team confirmed that the stream in Willow Room will have captions. I will meet you at the product demonstration afterwards.
Leon, 8:49 a.m.: Great. I have downloaded the sample files and will bring my laptop.

passages.label: D1
passages.text:
Oakline Learning: Junior content assistant
We are seeking a part-time assistant to prepare short website articles and simple promotional images. The role begins on 8 September and involves three mornings each week: Monday, Wednesday and Friday, from 9 a.m. to noon. During the first month, all work will take place at our office. After training, one of the three mornings may be worked remotely.
Applicants should be comfortable with basic image-editing tools and able to organise information clearly. A particular degree is not required. Experience with a content-management system is useful but can be developed on the job. Apply by 20 August with a résumé and a link to a portfolio containing two examples of your work. Our application system cannot accept attachments larger than ten megabytes.

passages.label: D2
passages.text:
From: Mira Santos
Sent: 18 August
Subject: Content assistant application
I created posters and short articles for my college club and have used several image-editing tools. My résumé uploaded successfully, but the system rejected my twelve-megabyte portfolio file. Could I send it another way? I have not used your content-management system before, but I would be happy to learn.
My current temporary job finishes on 1 September. Until then, I am free only on Tuesday and Thursday mornings. After that date, I can attend on all the mornings listed in the advertisement. Please let me know if you need my college transcript.

passages.label: D3
passages.text:
From: Oakline recruitment team
Sent: 19 August
Dear Mira,
Thank you for your message. Please upload your work to a site that allows viewing through a link, and send us that link by the advertised deadline. We do not need a transcript at this stage. Your experience with image-editing tools is relevant, and we provide training on our content-management system. Once we receive the portfolio link, we can confirm an online interview on a Tuesday or Thursday morning. The meeting link will follow in the confirmation message.
Best wishes,
Recruitment team

passages.label: A
passages.text: My name is Mai. I have a blue bag. My bag is on the chair. There is a book in it. The book is about cats. I have a yellow pencil and a red ruler too. My lunch box is under the desk. It is green. My friend Sam has a black bag. He has two books. We sit near the window. At lunch, we put our books on the desk and take our boxes to the garden.

passages.label: A
passages.text: It is Sunday. I am in the kitchen with Grandpa. He has a cup of tea. I have milk in a small glass. There are three eggs on a plate. Grandpa eats one egg and I eat two. We have bread too. My sister is in the garden with Mum. She does not want eggs. She wants a banana. I put one on her plate. After breakfast, Grandpa and I wash the cups. Then we go outside to see Mum.

passages.label: A
passages.text: This is my room. My toy shelf is next to my bed. A brown bear is on the top shelf. A little train is below the bear. My ball is on the floor. It is not on the shelf because it is too big. I have a red kite behind the door. My brother likes the train, but I like the kite. We take the kite to the park on windy days. Today there is no wind, so we play with the train.

passages.label: A
passages.text: Dad and I walk to a small pond. We see a duck in the water. There are two birds in a tree. A frog sits on a stone near the pond. It is green. I want to touch the frog, but Dad says no. We watch it quietly. The frog jumps into the water. Then we sit on the grass and draw the animals. Dad draws the duck. I draw the frog. We take our paper home and leave the pond clean.

passages.label: A
passages.text: It is a rainy afternoon. Linh and her cousin are at home. They cannot play in the yard. Linh looks for her yellow boots. They are beside the door. Her cousin has a blue coat and a red umbrella. They ask Linh's mum to walk with them. Mum says they can go when the rain stops. While they wait, they make a picture of the sun. Linh draws a big circle. Her cousin colours it orange. Soon the sky is bright, and they all go outside.

passages.label: A
passages.text: Ben goes to the library on Tuesday. He wants a story about a dragon. The librarian helps him find one on a low shelf. Ben opens his bag to get his library card, but the card is not there. He checks a pocket in his jacket. There is a bus ticket, but no card. Then his friend Hana points to an old book in his bag. Ben brought it to return today. The card is between two pages! Ben smiles and thanks her. He borrows the dragon story for one week. Before leaving, he puts the card in a small pocket in his bag so he can find it next time.

passages.label: A
passages.text: Our class has a bean plant near the window. Every morning, two children check it. On Monday, Eva touches the soil. It is dry, so she adds a little water. Minh measures the plant with a ruler. It is twelve centimetres tall. He writes the number in our plant diary. On Friday, the plant is fifteen centimetres tall and has one new leaf. We are excited. We do not move it to the dark cupboard because it needs light. Next week, another pair of children will care for it. Everyone wants a turn, and our teacher writes our names on a list.

passages.label: A
passages.text: Our family is planning a picnic for Saturday. We will meet Aunt Rose at the park gate at ten. Dad will bring a blanket, and Mum will bring sandwiches. I will pack four apples and some water. My little brother wants to bring his toy boat because there is a small lake. Mum says the boat must stay at home: we are going to the playground, not the lake. We will eat under a big tree after playing. If it rains, Aunt Rose will come to our house instead. We can have our picnic on the living-room floor and play a board game.

passages.label: A
passages.text: At sports day, Noor and Alex are in a short race. They wait behind the white line. The teacher blows a whistle, and everyone starts running. Noor is fast, but one of her shoes comes off. She stops to put it on. Alex is next to her. He asks if she is all right, then continues running. A girl called Jo reaches the finish first. Noor finishes last, but she is smiling. She says she enjoyed the race and is glad Alex checked on her. After the race, the teacher gives every runner some water. They sit in the shade and cheer for the next group.

passages.label: A
passages.text: Maya and her brother make a shop from a large cardboard box. They draw a sign and write 'Maya's Fruit Shop' on it. They use paper to make oranges, pears and grapes. Maya gives each fruit a price. A pear costs two toy coins, and an orange costs three. Their father is the first customer. He chooses two pears and gives Maya five coins. She gives him one coin back. Her brother puts the paper fruit in a bag. Later, they change jobs so he can be the shopkeeper. At the end of the afternoon, they put all the coins in a jar for their next game.

passages.label: A
passages.text:
Dear students,
Our new lunch club starts next Wednesday in Room 12. We meet from 12:15 to 12:45. Bring your own lunch and a bottle of water. You do not need to buy special food. We want to talk about meals from different homes and learn some simple food words in English. On the first day, Ms Lee will bring pictures of her favourite dishes. There will be no cooking because the room does not have a cooker.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The club is free, but there are only fifteen seats. Please write your name on the list outside the school office by Monday. If the list is full, put your name on the waiting list below it. We may open a second group on Friday. Students from all classes are welcome. You can come with a friend or meet someone new. Please leave the room tidy after lunch so the next class can use it.

passages.label: A
passages.text:
Hi An,
Music practice is at the community centre this Saturday, not at school. The school hall is being painted. Please bring your guitar and your music folder. We will start at ten and finish at half past eleven. Our teacher will wait at the centre's front entrance from 9:40.

passages.label: B
passages.text:
The number 8 bus stops outside the centre. It leaves our usual stop at 9:10 and takes twenty minutes to get there. The next bus leaves at 9:50, so it is too late for the start. I will take the 9:10 bus with my sister. She wants to visit the small bookshop beside the centre while we practise. After the lesson, Dad will drive us home. There is space for you in the car too. Please send me a message on Friday if you want a ride. You can also bring a snack, but we must eat outside the music room.
See you soon,
Bao

passages.label: A
passages.text: Last week, Minh forgot to finish his science homework. He did the easy questions first and then played a game. When he looked at the clock again, it was nearly bedtime. On Monday, his teacher helped him make a plan. First, he wrote all his tasks in a notebook. Beside each task, he put the day it was due. He also wrote down his football practice times so he could see when he was busy.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Now Minh checks the notebook after school. He begins with the work that needs to be ready soon. After twenty minutes, he takes a short break and walks around the house. He keeps his phone in another room while he works. His plan is not the same every day. On football days, he does less homework before dinner and more after dinner. He still has time for games, but he starts them only after he checks his completed work.

passages.label: A
passages.text: Our school has a book exchange table near the main stairs. Students can leave a book and take a different one. There is no money involved. The books should be clean, complete and suitable for students aged eleven to fifteen. Please do not bring books with missing pages or school library stamps. Those library books must go back to the library.

passages.label: B
passages.text: I brought an adventure book last Friday. I enjoyed it, but I wanted to try something new. On the table, I found a book about drawing animals. There was a short note inside it: 'Start with simple shapes and practise a little every day.' I took the book home and drew a fox. On Monday, I showed my picture to the art teacher. She asked where I had found the book. Now she wants to put a small box of drawing paper beside the exchange table. Students will be able to take a sheet and try a picture before choosing a book.

passages.label: A
passages.text: At coding club, our team built a small robot to carry an empty cup across a table. We marked a route with black tape and placed a cardboard bridge halfway along it. The robot followed the tape well, but it stopped whenever it reached the bridge. At first, we thought the battery was weak. We changed it, but the problem stayed.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Then Sara noticed that the bridge made a dark shadow over the tape. Our robot used a light sensor to find the black line. Under the bridge, it could not tell the line from the shadow. We moved the lamp, and the robot began to work again. However, the lamp would not be available during the club's final demonstration. We therefore changed the route so it went around the bridge. This made the journey longer but more reliable. In our presentation, we explained the problem and both solutions. We did not win the prize for speed, but another team asked to borrow our idea for avoiding difficult areas.

passages.label: A
passages.text: Our geography teacher asked us to make a map that would help new students find useful places near school. Our neighbourhood has several useful public places. We already had an online map, but it did not show everything we needed. For example, it showed the library entrance on River Road, although students had to use a side entrance after four o'clock. We decided to walk around the area in small groups with an adult and check the details ourselves.

passages.label: B
passages.text: My group visited the library, the sports centre and two bus stops. We wrote down opening times and looked for places where people could cross the road safely. At the sports centre, a member of staff showed us a ramp beside the steps. We added that to our map because some visitors might find it easier to use. Back at school, we compared our notes. Where two groups had different information, we phoned the place to check. The final map included a date so readers would know when we had collected the information. Our teacher said we should review it each term.

passages.label: A
passages.text: Lena's class wanted to make a ten-minute podcast about school life. They first planned to record it in the playground because they wanted lively background sounds. Their test recording, however, was full of wind noise and football whistles. Listeners could hardly hear the speakers. The class moved to an empty classroom and closed the windows during interviews.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The team shared the work. Lena prepared questions, Omar recorded the sound, and Nhi edited the programme. They asked the school gardener about a new vegetable bed and interviewed two students who had joined the chess club. Before recording, they explained where the podcast would appear and asked each guest for permission. One student agreed to speak but did not want their full name used. The team respected this request. After editing, the episode lasted fourteen minutes, so they removed repeated information rather than speaking faster. Their teacher listened to the final version before it went on the school website. The class kept a list of ideas for the next episode, including an interview with the cafeteria team.

passages.label: A
passages.text: Our class is going to a one-night nature camp at Willow Farm. The farm will provide tents and sleeping mats, but each student must bring a sleeping bag. We also need a waterproof jacket, a torch and a reusable water bottle. Phones can be used to contact families in the evening, but they should stay in bags during group activities. The teachers will carry a first-aid kit.

passages.label: B
passages.text: I began packing on Thursday, two days before the trip. At first, I put three heavy books in my bag because I like reading before bed. Then I read the schedule: a farm tour, a short walk, dinner and a storytelling circle. There was little free time, so I chose one thin book instead. I also checked my torch. It worked, but the light was weak, so I replaced the batteries. Finally, I put my name on my bottle and jacket. Last year, I lost a blue jacket because four other students had similar ones. This time I wanted to make my things easy to recognise.

passages.label: A
passages.text: At last year's school fair, the rubbish bins were full before lunchtime. This year, the student council wanted to change that. They asked each stall to avoid small plastic prizes and unnecessary wrapping. The craft stall offered bookmarks made from leftover card, and the games stall gave winners stamps on a paper passport. Five stamps could be exchanged for a plant grown by the gardening club.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The drinks stall was more difficult. The council suggested asking everyone to bring a cup, but they knew some visitors would forget. They arranged a small collection of washable cups that people could borrow for a deposit. When visitors returned a cup, they received their deposit back. Two volunteers washed the cups at a kitchen sink. At the end of the day, the bins still contained rubbish, so the council did not call the fair waste-free. However, the staff needed fewer rubbish bags than before. The students wrote down what worked and what caused queues so they could improve the plan next year.

passages.label: A
passages.text: For our class exhibition, the art teacher asked us to bring an ordinary object with a story behind it. The object did not need to be valuable. It had to be safe to display, and we needed permission if it belonged to someone else. I chose a scratched wooden spoon that my grandfather had made. My mother still used it for mixing cake batter, so I brought a photograph of it instead of the real spoon.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Each student wrote a short label explaining the object's story. Lan displayed a train ticket from her first trip alone to visit her aunt. Daniel brought a repaired football that his cousins had used for years. At first, we arranged everything by size. Then we realised that visitors would understand more if we grouped the objects by theme: journeys, family, hobbies and learning. We left space between the displays and printed the labels in large letters. During the exhibition, a visitor asked why a simple spoon deserved a place. After reading its label, she told me that her own family had a favourite kitchen tool too.

passages.label: A
passages.text: When our school announced a repair desk, some students expected a free service that would fix any broken object. The organisers had a different aim: they wanted people to learn simple repair skills alongside experienced volunteers. For safety reasons, the desk accepted torn bags, loose buttons and damaged book covers, but not electrical equipment. Visitors booked a twenty-minute slot and described their problem in advance so the team could prepare suitable materials.

passages.label: B
passages.text: I brought a backpack with a broken zip. The volunteer inspected it and explained that the entire zip would need replacing. That task was too long for our appointment, and the correct replacement was not available. Instead of pretending there was an easy solution, she showed me how to stop the tear beside the zip from growing. She also wrote down the measurements I would need when buying a replacement. At first, I felt disappointed because my bag was not completely fixed. Then I realised I had learned how to describe the problem and decide what to do next.

passages.label: C
passages.text: After the first month, the organisers considered measuring success by counting repaired items. However, this would ignore visits like mine. They added a short feedback form asking what visitors had learned and whether they felt more confident making small repairs. The desk still recorded completed repairs, but learning became a separate goal. It was a modest project, yet its value extended beyond the objects that left looking new. Several students returned later as helpers, bringing skills they had practised at home.

passages.label: A
passages.text: On Sunday evening, a screenshot appeared in our class chat. It seemed to announce that Monday's lessons would move online because of building work. The message included the school logo, and several students immediately began changing their plans. However, the screenshot did not show a date or a link to the original announcement. Our class representative, Huy, asked everyone to wait before sharing it further.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Huy opened the school's official notice page and found no new message about online lessons. He then searched older notices and discovered an announcement with almost the same wording from the previous year. At that time, repairs had closed one part of the building for a day. Someone had cropped the old notice so that its date was invisible. Huy could not tell whether this had been done as a joke or whether the person who first shared it had made an honest mistake. He therefore explained what was wrong with the image without accusing a particular student.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The teacher later confirmed that Monday's classes would take place as usual. In the next lesson, we discussed why the screenshot had seemed believable. The logo created a sense of authority, while the practical importance of the message encouraged us to act quickly. We agreed that checking information did not mean rejecting every surprising claim. It meant finding the original source, checking when it was published and looking for confirmation when the consequences mattered. A classmate suggested keeping a direct link to official notices at the top of the chat so that checking would be easier next time.

passages.label: A
passages.text: A group of students proposed turning an unused corner of the playground into an outdoor study area. Their first design included bright benches and large decorative pots. Before spending the entire budget, the deputy head asked them to test whether students would actually use the space. The group borrowed two folding tables and placed them beneath an existing tree for a week. They invited students to leave comments on a simple paper form.

passages.label: B
passages.text: At lunchtime, the tables were popular, but not always for studying. Some students ate there, while others chatted or played cards. During afternoon free periods, the corner was quieter, although one table received direct sunlight. Several students also pointed out that bags had to be left on the ground. The project team originally regarded these comments as complaints about a nearly finished plan. After discussing them, they realised the trial had revealed needs they had overlooked. The revised design included a shelf for bags and a movable shade screen. They also proposed separate quiet hours rather than trying to make the area silent all day.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The school approved a smaller first purchase so the team could make further changes after another trial. This disappointed students who wanted the full design installed immediately. Yet the team preferred to improve a useful space gradually rather than spend the whole budget on an attractive area that failed to suit daily routines. Their final presentation showed both the original sketch and the revised version. The differences became evidence of learning rather than something to hide from the audience.

passages.label: A
passages.text: When I was offered a weekend job at a small bookshop, I focused on the money I could save for a new laptop. The owner needed someone to arrange shelves, wrap books and help customers find the collection point for online orders. I would work on both Saturday and Sunday afternoons. My parents did not reject the idea, but they asked me to write down everything else I needed to do during a normal week.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The list was longer than I expected. Apart from lessons and homework, I had basketball practice, a group science project and a regular visit to my grandmother. I initially assumed I could simply work faster. However, a classmate who had already taken a part-time job suggested including travel time and rest in the plan. Once I added these, almost every hour of my weekend was occupied. I returned to the bookshop and asked whether I could begin with one afternoon instead of two. The owner agreed to a one-month trial because another employee wanted the remaining shift.

passages.label: C
passages.text: During the trial, I learned useful customer-service skills and saved a smaller amount than I had first imagined. I also discovered that homework requiring concentration was harder after a busy shift. I began doing that work on Saturday morning, before going to the shop. At the end of the month, I decided to continue with one afternoon. The job was worthwhile, but only when its demands fitted the rest of my life. Earning the maximum possible amount was no longer my only measure of success.

passages.label: A
passages.text: Our local museum invited secondary students to design a display about the old market street. The museum already held photographs of shop fronts and records of important building changes. We expected to select the clearest photographs, add dates and arrange everything in order. Then our teacher asked a question: whose experiences would visitors hear if we used only those materials? The records said little about people who had worked behind the counters or delivered goods before dawn.

passages.label: B
passages.text: With the museum's help, we interviewed former market workers. One retired baker described sharing an oven with a neighbouring stall when his own had broken. A delivery worker remembered which narrow lane stayed dry during heavy rain. These accounts added practical details that the photographs could not show. However, memories were not always precise. Two people gave different years for the same street celebration. Instead of choosing the more confident speaker, we checked a dated newspaper report held by the museum. Where a detail remained uncertain, we said so on the label.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The final display combined official records with short personal accounts, used with the speakers' permission. We also included a blank map on which visitors could suggest places for future research. Some students had worried that admitting uncertainty would make our work look weak. In practice, it helped visitors understand how historical knowledge was assembled. The display did not claim to tell every person's story. It offered a wider view of the street and made clear which voices and questions still needed attention. For us, designing an exhibition became an exercise in listening as well as selecting attractive images.

passages.label: A
passages.text: When the town library extended its opening hours, the staff expected users to welcome the change. Many did, but complaints about noise increased. Students preparing for examinations wanted silence, while language learners needed a place to practise conversation. Parents with young children appreciated shared reading sessions, and some older visitors came partly for social contact. Treating all these activities as disturbances would have excluded people the library was intended to serve.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The staff initially considered dividing the building into a quiet floor and a social floor. However, the only accessible toilet and the children's collection were both on the ground floor, where some quiet readers also preferred to sit. A strict division by floor would therefore create new difficulties. After a period of consultation, the library introduced smaller zones and clear time periods for particular activities. One enclosed room became a conversation space in the afternoon and a silent study room in the evening. Signs explained the purpose of each zone without suggesting that one type of visitor was more deserving than another.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The arrangement did not eliminate every disagreement. A study group sometimes forgot to lower its voices, and visitors occasionally arrived expecting an activity that was not scheduled that day. Staff treated these incidents as reasons to improve communication, rather than evidence that shared use was impossible. They displayed the weekly timetable at the entrance and asked users to comment after a month. The experience suggested that fairness did not require identical conditions everywhere. It required making different needs visible and designing rules that people could understand. The library's success depended less on finding one perfect rule than on continuing to adjust the arrangement as its community changed.

passages.label: A
passages.text: The school cafeteria often faced the same dilemma: preparing too much food created leftovers, while preparing too little disappointed students who arrived later. A student data club offered to help estimate demand. Its members began by recording how many meals were sold each day, which dishes were offered and whether major school events were taking place. They avoided collecting individual students' names because the project concerned total demand, not personal eating habits.

passages.label: B
passages.text: After several weeks, the club noticed patterns. Some dishes sold more consistently than others, and attendance at lunchtime changed during examination periods. Their first prediction method simply used the average sales for the same dish on previous occasions. To see whether it helped, they tested it on days that had not been used to calculate the averages. The results were mixed. Predictions were usually closer than a fixed daily target, but an unexpected sports cancellation left far more students eating at school than usual. The club presented this failure alongside its successes.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Rather than promising an exact number, the students began offering a likely range and listing events that might change demand. The cafeteria manager used this information together with her own knowledge of preparation times and available ingredients. She also kept a small reserve of items that could be prepared quickly. Less food was left over during the next trial, but the club did not attribute the entire improvement to its calculations: menu changes and the manager's adjustments had occurred at the same time. The project taught students that a useful prediction supports judgement. It does not remove uncertainty or replace the person responsible for a decision.

passages.label: A
passages.text: For a history project, our group asked an AI writing tool to explain why a small local railway station had closed. The response was fluent and included three apparent references. It seemed to offer a convenient starting point. Yet when we searched for the first reference in the library catalogue, we could not find it. The second named a real local newspaper but gave no publication date. Only the third led to a document we could actually inspect, and that document did not support the explanation the tool had given.

passages.label: B
passages.text: We could have abandoned the tool completely, but our teacher suggested examining which tasks it could still help with. We used it to suggest search terms, organise questions for an interview and rewrite a sentence we had already checked for clarity. For claims about the station, however, we returned to council records and archived newspaper reports. We kept a table linking each important statement to a source we had read ourselves. When sources disagreed, we described the disagreement instead of asking the tool to choose whichever account sounded smoother.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The experience changed our idea of efficiency. A polished paragraph produced in seconds was not necessarily useful if checking it took longer than doing the original research. On the other hand, suggestions for organising notes saved time without being treated as historical evidence. In our final presentation, we described how we had used the tool and which checks we had made. The main lesson was to match the tool to the task. Fluency could help communication, but it could not establish that a factual claim was true. Responsibility for the report remained with the students whose names appeared on it.

passages.label: A
passages.text: The environmental club wanted to compare bird activity at two ponds near the school. Members designed a simple observation sheet listing the time, weather and number of birds they could see during a ten-minute period. They agreed to watch from fixed positions and avoid feeding the birds. The aim was to describe activity under the observed conditions, rather than to count every bird living in the area.

passages.label: B
passages.text: After three weeks, Pond A appeared busier than Pond B. Several students were ready to conclude that its habitat was better. However, when the group examined the observation sheets, an important difference emerged. Most visits to Pond A had taken place early in the morning, while Pond B was usually visited after school because it was farther away. Rainy afternoons had also been skipped. The two sets of observations therefore differed in more than location. A larger total at one pond might reflect the visiting schedule rather than a stable difference between the sites.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The club revised its plan. Small teams would visit both ponds at matching times on selected days, accompanied by a teacher. They would record unsuccessful visits and reasons for missing data instead of silently leaving those days out. They also decided to report the number of observation periods alongside their totals. This did not make the survey perfect: birds could still hide behind vegetation, and short visits could miss changes during the rest of the day. Nevertheless, the revised method made the comparison easier to interpret. The students learned that collecting more numbers was not enough. They also needed to understand how the numbers had been produced and which conclusions the design could reasonably support.

passages.label: A
passages.text: At a school careers event, three former students described different routes into work. One had completed a university degree, another was doing an apprenticeship, and the third had combined a short vocational course with employment. The audience initially treated the talks as a competition to identify the best route. Each speaker, however, explained that the usefulness of a route depended on the occupation, the quality of the programme and the learner's circumstances.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The apprentice described gaining practical experience while studying, but also mentioned the difficulty of managing assignments after a working day. The graduate valued time for broad study and access to particular professional opportunities, while acknowledging the financial commitment involved. The third speaker emphasised the speed of starting paid work, yet warned that a short course might not cover everything needed for future roles. None presented their own decision as suitable for everyone. Their accounts made the trade-offs more visible than the course advertisements students had collected earlier.

passages.label: C
passages.text: After the event, our class created a comparison sheet. Instead of ranking options by reputation alone, we listed entry requirements, total costs, supervised practice, recognised qualifications and possibilities for further study. We also noted which details were still uncertain and who could verify them. A teacher reminded us that a confident presentation was not a substitute for checking the actual programme. The exercise did not produce one answer for the entire class. It produced better questions. Some students kept their original plans but could explain them more clearly; others arranged visits to explore alternatives. Choosing a path became a process of matching evidence to personal goals, rather than accepting a label that happened to sound impressive.
